{{Short description|2015–2016 public relations and legal dispute}}
{{Use American English|date=February 2016}}
{{Use mdy dates|date=March 2016}}

[[File:IPhone 5c blue back.jpg|thumb|alt=Rear side of blue iPhone 5c.|right|An [[iPhone 5C]] (color), the model used by one of the perpetrators of the [[2015 San Bernardino attack]]]]

The '''Apple–FBI encryption dispute''' concerns whether and to what extent courts in the [[United States]] can compel manufacturers to assist in unlocking [[cell phone]]s whose [[data]] are [[Cryptography|cryptographically protected]].<ref>{{cite magazine|url=https://time.com/4262480/tim-cook-apple-fbi-2/|title=Inside Apple CEO Tim Cook's Fight With the FBI|first=Lev|last=Grossman|magazine=Time|date=March 17, 2016|access-date=March 17, 2016|archive-date=February 10, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210210092022/https://time.com/4262480/tim-cook-apple-fbi-2/|url-status=live}}</ref> There is much debate over public access to [[strong encryption]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2016/03/29/technology/apple-iphone-fbi-justice-department-case.html|title=U.S. Says It Has Unlocked iPhone Without Apple|first1=Katie|last1=Benner|first2=Eric|last2=Lichtblau|work=The New York Times|date=March 28, 2016|access-date=March 28, 2016|archive-date=February 10, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210210092017/https://www.nytimes.com/2016/03/29/technology/apple-iphone-fbi-justice-department-case.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

In 2015 and 2016, [[Apple Inc.]] received and objected to or challenged at least 11 orders issued by [[United States district court]]s under the [[All Writs Act]] of 1789. Most of these seek to compel Apple "to use its existing capabilities to extract data like contacts, photos and calls from locked [[iPhone]]s running on operating systems [[iOS 7]] and older" in order to assist in criminal investigations and prosecutions. A few requests, however, involve phones with more extensive security protections, which Apple has no current ability to break. These orders would compel Apple to write new software that would let the government bypass these devices' security and unlock the phones.<ref name="McLaughlin">{{cite web|url=https://theintercept.com/2016/02/23/new-court-filing-reveals-apple-faces-12-other-requests-to-break-into-locked-iphones/|title=New Court Filing Reveals Apple Faces 12 Other Requests to Break Into Locked iPhones|work=The Intercept|date=February 23, 2016|access-date=March 3, 2016|first=Jenna|last=McLaughlin|archive-date=February 10, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210210092002/https://theintercept.com/2016/02/23/new-court-filing-reveals-apple-faces-12-other-requests-to-break-into-locked-iphones/|url-status=live}}</ref>

The most well-known instance of the latter category was a February 2016 court case in the [[United States District Court for the Central District of California]]. The [[Federal Bureau of Investigation]] (FBI) wanted Apple to create and [[digital signature|electronically sign]] new software that would enable the FBI to unlock a work-issued [[iPhone 5C]] it recovered from one of the shooters who, in [[2015 San Bernardino attack|a December 2015 terrorist attack]] in [[San Bernardino, California]], killed 14 people and injured 22. The two attackers later died in a shootout with police, having first destroyed their personal phones. The work phone was recovered intact but was locked with a four-digit passcode and was set to eliminate all its data after ten failed password attempts (a common anti-theft measure on smartphones). Apple declined to create the software, and a hearing was scheduled for March 22. However, a day before the hearing was supposed to happen, the government obtained a delay, saying it had found a third party able to assist in unlocking the iPhone. On March 28, the government claimed that the FBI had unlocked the iPhone and withdrew its request. In March 2018, the ''[[Los Angeles Times]]'' reported "the FBI eventually found that Farook's phone had information only about work and revealed nothing about the plot" but cited only government claims, not evidence.<ref name="access delayed">{{Cite news|url=http://www.latimes.com/politics/la-na-pol-fbi-iphone-san-bernardino-20180327-story.html|title=Race to unlock San Bernardino shooter's iPhone was delayed by poor FBI communication, report finds|last=Tanfani|first=Joseph|date=March 27, 2018|work=Los Angeles Times|access-date=August 18, 2018|archive-date=July 22, 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180722011321/http://www.latimes.com/politics/la-na-pol-fbi-iphone-san-bernardino-20180327-story.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

In another case in Brooklyn, a magistrate judge ruled that the [[All Writs Act]] could not be used to compel Apple to unlock an iPhone. The government appealed the ruling, but then dropped the case on April 22, 2016, saying it had been given the correct passcode.<ref>{{Cite news|last=Lichtblau|first=Eric|date=2016-04-23|title=U.S. Opens Another iPhone, This Time With the Keycode|language=en-US|work=The New York Times|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2016/04/23/business/us-opens-another-iphone-this-time-with-the-pacode.html|access-date=2021-04-16|issn=0362-4331}}</ref>

== Background ==
{{Main|Crypto Wars}}
[[File:James Comey official portrait.jpg|thumb|upright|[[James Comey]], former [[Director of the Federal Bureau of Investigation|FBI director]]]]
[[File:Visit of Tim Cook to the European Commission - P061904-946789.jpg|thumb|upright|[[Tim Cook]], former Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of [[Apple Inc.]] Cook and former FBI director Comey have both spoken publicly about the case.]]

In 1993, the [[National Security Agency]] (NSA) introduced the [[Clipper chip]], an encryption device with an acknowledged [[backdoor (computing)|backdoor]] for government access, that NSA proposed be used for phone encryption. The proposal touched off a public debate, known as the [[Crypto Wars]], and the Clipper chip was never adopted.<ref>[[Crypto: How the Code Rebels Beat the Government—Saving Privacy in the Digital Age]], Steven Levy, 2001</ref>

It was revealed as a part of the [[Global surveillance disclosures (2013–present)|2013 mass surveillance disclosures]] by [[Edward Snowden]] that the NSA and the British [[Government Communications Headquarters]] (GCHQ) had access to the user data in iPhones, [[BlackBerry]], and [[Android (operating system)|Android]] phones and could read almost all smartphone information, including SMS, location, emails, and notes.<ref name="spiegel20130907">{{cite news|url=http://www.spiegel.de/international/world/a-920971.html|title=Privacy Scandal: NSA Can Spy on Smart Phone Data|date=September 7, 2013|access-date=February 25, 2016|archive-date=September 19, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190919033145/https://www.spiegel.de/international/world/privacy-scandal-nsa-can-spy-on-smart-phone-data-a-920971.html|url-status=live}}</ref> Additionally, the leak stated that Apple had been a part of the [[PRISM (surveillance program)|government's surveillance program]] since 2012, however, Apple per their spokesman at the time, "had never heard of it".<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/2013/06/06/nsa-surveillance-internet-companies/2398345/|title=NSA taps data from 9 major Net firms|website=USA Today|language=en|access-date=2019-05-05|archive-date=June 7, 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130607113440/http://www.usatoday.com/story/news/2013/06/06/nsa-surveillance-internet-companies/2398345/|url-status=live}}</ref>

According to ''[[The New York Times]]'', Apple developed new encryption methods for its [[iOS]] operating system, versions 8 and later, "so deep that Apple could no longer comply with government warrants asking for customer information to be extracted from devices."<ref name=postsnowden>{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2014/09/27/technology/iphone-locks-out-the-nsa-signaling-a-post-snowden-era-.html|title=Signaling Post-Snowden Era, New iPhone Locks Out N.S.A.|date=September 27, 2014|access-date=February 25, 2016|first1=David E.|last1=Sanger|first2=Brian X.|last2=Chen|work=The New York Times|archive-date=February 10, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210210092014/https://www.nytimes.com/2014/09/27/technology/iphone-locks-out-the-nsa-signaling-a-post-snowden-era-.html|url-status=live}}</ref> Throughout 2015, prosecutors advocated for the U.S. government to be able to compel decryption of iPhone contents.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.wired.com/2015/07/manhattan-da-iphone-crypto-foiled-cops-74-times/|title=Manhattan DA: iPhone Crypto Locked Out Cops 74 Times|date=July 8, 2015|access-date=February 25, Probes|first1=Tiffany|last1=Kary|first2=Chris|last2=Dolmetsch|date=November 18, 2015|work=Bloomberg News|access-date=February 25, 2016}}</ref>

In September 2015, Apple released a white paper detailing the security measures in its then-new [[iOS 9]] operating system. iPhone models including the [[iPhone 5C]] can be protected by a four-digit [[Personal identification number|PIN]] code. After more than ten incorrect attempts to unlock the phone with the wrong PIN, the contents of the phone will be rendered inaccessible by erasing the [[Advanced Encryption Standard|AES]] [[encryption key]] that protects its stored data. According to the Apple white paper, iOS includes a [[Device Firmware Upgrade]] (DFU) mode, and that "[r]estoring a device after it enters DFU mode returns it to a known good state with the certainty that only unmodified Apple-signed code is present."<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.apple.com/business/docs/iOS_Security_Guide.pdf|title=iOS Security—Version 9 or later|work=Apple Inc.|date=September 2015|access-date=February 25, 2016|archive-date=February 27, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160227071343/http://www.apple.com/business/docs/iOS_Security_Guide.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref>

== Apple ordered to assist the FBI ==
The FBI recovered an Apple [[iPhone 5C]]—owned by the [[San Bernardino County, California]] government—that had been issued to its employee, [[Rizwan Farook and Tashfeen Malik|Syed Rizwan Farook]], one of the shooters involved in the December [[2015 San Bernardino attack]].<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/world/national-security/us-wants-apple-to-help-unlock-iphone-used-by-san-bernardino-shooter/2016/02/16/69b903ee-d4d9-11e5-9823-02b905009f99_story.html|title=Apple vows to resist FBI demand to crack iPhone linked to San Bernardino attacks|newspaper=The Washington Post|date=February 17, 2016|access-date=February 18, 2016|first=Ellen|last=Nakashima|archive-date=February 17, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160217224411/https://www.washingtonpost.com/world/national-security/us-wants-apple-to-help-unlock-iphone-used-by-san-bernardino-shooter/2016/02/16/69b903ee-d4d9-11e5-9823-02b905009f99_story.html|url-status=live}}</ref> The attack killed 14 people and seriously injured 22. The two attackers died four hours after the attack in a shootout with police, having previously destroyed their personal phones. Authorities were able to recover Farook's work phone, but could not unlock its four-digit passcode,<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.documentcloud.org/documents/2716000-031122954861.html | title=Government's Motion to Compel Apple Inc. to Comply With This Court's February 16, 2016 Order Compelling Assistance in Search | date=February 19, 2016 | first1=Eileen M. | last1=Decker | first2=Patricia A. | last2=Donahue | first3=Tracy L. | last3=Wilkison | first4=Allen W. | last4=Chiu | work=United States Attorneys | access-date=February 27, 2016 | archive-date=February 10, 2021 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210210092005/https://www.documentcloud.org/documents/2716000-031122954861.html | url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last1=Zetter|first1=Kim|title=New Documents Solve a Few Mysteries in the Apple-FBI Saga|url=https://www.wired.com/2016/03/new-documents-solve-mysteries-apple-fbi-saga/|access-date=March 11, 2016|publisher=WIRED|date=March 11, 2016|archive-date=February 10, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210210092010/https://www.wired.com/2016/03/new-documents-solve-mysteries-apple-fbi-saga/|url-status=live}}</ref> and the phone was programmed to automatically delete all its data after ten failed password attempts.

On February 9, 2016, the FBI announced that it was unable to unlock the county-owned phone it recovered, due to its advanced security features, including encryption of user data.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-california-shooting-encryption-idUSKCN0VI22A|title=FBI director says investigators unable to unlock San Bernardino shooter's phone content|work=Reuters|date=February 9, 2016|access-date=March 31, 2016|first1=Dustin|last1=Volz|first2=Mark|last2=Hosenball|archive-date=February 17, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160217161620/http://www.reuters.com/article/us-california-shooting-encryption-idUSKCN0VI22A|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.pressenterprise.com/2016/02/16/san-bernardino-shooting-apple-ordered-help-us-hack-killer8217s-phone/|title=SAN BERNARDINO SHOOTING: Apple must help US hack killer's phone|work=The Press-Enterprise|date=February 16, 2016|access-date=February 16, 2016|first1=Tami|last1=Abdollah|first2=Eric|last2=Tucker|archive-date=February 18, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160218092719/http://www.pe.com/articles/washington-794488-help-killer.html|url-status=live}}</ref> The FBI first asked the [[National Security Agency]] to break into the phone, but they were unable to since they only had knowledge of breaking into other devices that are commonly used by criminals, and not iPhones.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.zdnet.com/article/nsa-comes-clean-on-why-it-couldnt-hack-san-bernardino-shooters-iphone/|title=NSA finally admits why it couldn't hack San Bernardino shooter's iPhone|work=ZDNet|date=June 10, 2016|access-date=June 11, 2016|first=Zack|last=Whittaker|archive-date=February 10, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210210092225/https://www.zdnet.com/article/nsa-comes-clean-on-why-it-couldnt-hack-san-bernardino-shooters-iphone/|url-status=live}}</ref> As a result, the FBI asked [[Apple Inc.]] to create a new version of the phone's [[iOS]] [[operating system]] that could be installed and run in the phone's [[random access memory]] to disable certain security features that Apple refers to as "GovtOS". Apple declined due to its policy which required it to never undermine the security features of its products. The FBI responded by successfully applying to a [[United States magistrate judge]], Sheri Pym, to issue a court order, mandating Apple to create and provide the requested software.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nbcnews.com/storyline/san-bernardino-shooting/judge-forces-apple-help-unlock-san-bernardino-shooter-iphone-n519701|title=Judge Forces Apple to Help Unlock San Bernardino Shooter iPhone|work=NBC News|date=February 16, 2016|access-date=February 16, 2016|first=Andrew|last=Blankstein|archive-date=February 17, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160217043031/http://www.nbcnews.com/storyline/san-bernardino-shooting/judge-forces-apple-help-unlock-san-bernardino-shooter-iphone-n519701|url-status=live}}</ref> The order was not a [[subpoena]], but rather was issued under the [[All Writs Act of 1789]].<ref>{{cite web|first=Robert M.|last=Chesney|url=https://www.lawfaremedia.org/article/apple-vs-fbi-going-dark-dispute-moves-congress-courtroom|title=Apple vs FBI: The Going Dark Dispute Moves from Congress to the In the Matter of the Search of an Apple iPhone Seized During the Execution of a Search Warrant on a Black Lexus IS300, California License Plate 35KGD203|url=https://www.docketalarm.com/cases/California_Central_District_Court/5--16-cm-00010/USA_v._In_the_Matter_of_the_Search_of_an_Apple_iPhone_Seized_During_the_Execution_of_a_Search_Warrant_on_a_Black_Lexus_IS300_California_License_Plate_35KGD203/|publisher=Docket Alarm|access-date=March 16, 2016|archive-date=February 10, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210210092013/https://www.docketalarm.com/cases/California_Central_District_Court/5--16-cm-00010/USA_v._In_the_Matter_of_the_Search_of_an_Apple_iPhone_Seized_During_the_Execution_of_a_Search_Warrant_on_a_Black_Lexus_IS300_California_License_Plate_35KGD203/|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name=":0">{{cite web | url=https://assets.documentcloud.org/documents/2714005/SB-Shooter-Order-Compelling-Apple-Asst-iPhone.pdf | title=Order Compelling Apple, Inc. to Assist Agents in Search | date=February 16, 2016 | first=Sheri | last=Pym | publisher=United States District Court for the Central District of California | access-date=February 27, 2016 | archive-date=February 10, 2021 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210210091942/https://assets.documentcloud.org/documents/2714005/SB-Shooter-Order-Compelling-Apple-Asst-iPhone.pdf | url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|first=Edvard|last=Pettersson|url=https://www.bloomberg.com/politics/articles/2016-02-25/apple-says-u-s-can-t-force-it-to-unlock-terrorist-s-iphone-il2pjiw8|title=Apple Slams U.S. Bid to Make It Crack iPhone in Court Papers|work=Bloomberg Politics|date=February 25, 2016|access-date=February 25, 2016}}</ref>

The use of the [[All Writs Act]] to compel Apple to write new software was unprecedented and, according to legal experts, it was likely to prompt "an epic fight pitting privacy against national security."<ref name="DolanKimAllWrits">{{cite web|first1=Maura|last1=Dolan|first2=Victoria|last2=Kim|url=http://www.latimes.com/business/la-me-fbi-apple-legal-20160219-story.html|title=Apple-FBI fight over iPhone encryption pits privacy against national security|work=Los Angeles Times|date=February 18, 2016|access-date=February 20, 2016|archive-date=February 10, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210210092242/https://www.latimes.com/business/la-me-fbi-apple-legal-20160219-story.html|url-status=live}}</ref> It was also pointed out that the implications of the legal precedent that would be established by the success of this action against Apple would go far beyond issues of privacy.<ref>{{cite web|first=Amy|last=Davidson|url=http://www.newyorker.com/news/amy-davidson/a-dangerous-all-writ-precedent-in-the-apple-case|title=The Dangerous All Writs Act Precedent in the Apple Encryption Case|work=New Yorker|date=February 19, 2016|access-date=February 20, 2016|archive-date=February 10, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210210092226/https://www.newyorker.com/news/amy-davidson/a-dangerous-all-writ-precedent-in-the-apple-case|url-status=live}}</ref>

=== Technical details of the order ===
The court order specified that Apple provide assistance to accomplish the following:
# "it will bypass or disable the auto-erase function whether or not it has been enabled"<ref name=":0" /> (this user-configurable feature of iOS 8 automatically deletes keys needed to read encrypted data after ten consecutive incorrect attempts<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://assets.documentcloud.org/documents/2722199/5-15-MJ-00451-SP-USA-v-Black-Lexus-IS300.pdf|title=APPLE INC'S MOTION TO VACATE|last=Boutrous Jr.|first=Theodore J.|date=February 25, 2016|website=Documentcloud|page=51|access-date=March 14, 2016|archive-date=February 10, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210210091943/https://assets.documentcloud.org/documents/2722199/5-15-MJ-00451-SP-USA-v-Black-Lexus-IS300.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref>)
# "it will enable the FBI to submit passcodes to the SUBJECT DEVICE for testing electronically via the physical device port, Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, or other protocol available"<ref name=":0" />
# "it will ensure that when the FBI submits passcodes to the SUBJECT DEVICE, software running on the device will not purposefully introduce any additional delay between passcode attempts beyond what is incurred by Apple hardware"<ref name=":0" />
The order also specifies that Apple's assistance may include providing software to the FBI that "will be coded by Apple with a unique identifier of the phone so that the [software] would only load and execute on the SUBJECT DEVICE".<ref name=":0" />

There has been much research and analysis of the technical issues presented in the case since the court order was made available to the public.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.readysignon.com/step-step-technical-analysis-fbis-case-compelling-apple-unlock-san-bernardino-shooters-iphone/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160403122351/https://readysignon.com/step-step-technical-analysis-fbis-case-compelling-apple-unlock-san-bernardino-shooters-iphone/|url-status=dead|archive-date=April 3, 2016|title=Analyzing the FBI case against Apple: A technical review|work=ReadySignOn|access-date=March 21, 2016}}</ref>

=== Apple's opposition to the order ===
The February 16, 2016 order issued by Magistrate Judge Pym gave Apple five days to apply for relief if Apple believed the order was "unreasonably burdensome". Apple announced its intent to oppose the order, citing the security risks that the creation of a [[Backdoor (computing)|backdoor]] would pose towards customers.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.cnn.com/2016/02/16/us/san-bernardino-shooter-phone-apple/|title=Apple opposes judge's order to hack San Bernardino shooter's iPhone|publisher=CNN|date=February 17, 2016|access-date=February 17, 2016|first1=Evan|last1=Perez|first2=Tim|last2=Hume|archive-date=February 18, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160218092519/http://www.cnn.com/2016/02/16/us/san-bernardino-shooter-phone-apple/|url-status=live}}</ref> It also stated that no government had ever asked for similar access.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2016/feb/19/apple-fbi-encryption-battle-san-bernardino-shooting-syed-farook-iphone|title=Apple says the FBI is making access demands even China hasn't asked for|work=The Guardian|date=February 19, 2016|access-date=February 20, 2016|first=Danny|last=Yadron|archive-date=February 20, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160220042614/http://www.theguardian.com/technology/2016/feb/19/apple-fbi-encryption-battle-san-bernardino-shooting-syed-farook-iphone|url-status=live}}</ref> The company was given until February 26 to fully respond to the court order.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.pressenterprise.com/2016/02/19/san-bernardino-shooting-apple-gets-more-time-to-file-its-response/|title=SAN BERNARDINO SHOOTING: Apple gets more time to file its response|work=The web|url=https://money.cnn.com/2016/03/21/technology/apple-fbi-tuesday/index.html|title=Apple will battle the FBI in court Tuesday|last=Pagliery|first=Jose|work=CNN Money|date=March 21, 2016|access-date=April 20, 2016|archive-date=February 10, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210210092020/https://money.cnn.com/2016/03/21/technology/apple-fbi-tuesday/index.html|url-status=dead}}</ref>

On the same day the order was issued, [[chief executive officer]] [[Tim Cook]] released an online statement to Apple customers, explaining the company's motives for opposing the court order. He also stated that while they respect the FBI, the request they made threatens data security by establishing a precedent that the U.S. government could use to force any technology company to create software that could undermine the security of its products.<ref name=AppleCook>{{cite web|url=https://www.apple.com/customer-letter/|title=A Message to Our Customers|publisher=Apple Inc.|date=February 16, 2016|access-date=February 19, 2016|first=Tim|last=Cook|archive-date=February 17, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160217084120/http://www.apple.com/customer-letter/|url-status=live}}</ref> He said in part:

{{blockquote|The United States government has demanded that Apple take an unprecedented step which threatens the security of our customers. We oppose this order, which has implications far beyond the legal case at hand. This moment calls for public discussion, and we want our customers and people around the country to understand what is at stake.<ref name=AppleCook/>}}

In response to the opposition, on February 19, the [[United States Department of Justice|U.S. Department of Justice]] filed a new application urging a federal judge to compel Apple to comply with the order.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://abcnews.go.com/US/doj-escalates-battle-apple-san-bernardino-shooters-phone/story?id=37056775|title=DOJ Escalates Battle With Apple Over San Bernardino Shooter's Phone|work=ABC News|date=February 19, 2016|access-date=February 19, 2016|first1=Mike|last1=Levine|first2=Jack|last2=Date|first3=Jack|last3=Cloherty|archive-date=February 10, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210210092230/https://abcnews.go.com/US/doj-escalates-battle-apple-san-bernardino-shooters-phone/story?id=37056775|url-status=live}}</ref> The new application stated that the company could install the software on the phone in its own premises, and after the FBI had hacked the phone via remote connection, Apple could remove and destroy the software.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.scpr.org/news/2016/02/19/57752/san-bernardino-justice-department-files-new-motion|title=San Bernardino shooting: US says Apple could keep, destroy software to help FBI hack iPhone|agency=Associated Press|date=February 19, 2016|access-date=February 19, 2016|archive-date=February 20, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160220090543/http://www.scpr.org/news/2016/02/19/57752/san-bernardino-justice-department-files-new-motion/|url-status=live}}</ref> Apple hired attorneys [[Ted Olson]] and Theodore J. Boutrous Jr. to fight the order on appeal.<ref name="DolanKimAllWrits" />

The same day, Apple revealed that in early January it had discussed with the FBI four methods to access data in the iPhone, but, as was revealed by a footnote in the February 19 application to the court, one of the more promising methods was ruled out by a mistake during the investigation of the attack. After the shooter's phone had been recovered, the FBI asked San Bernardino County, the owner of the phone, to reset the password to the shooter's [[iCloud]] account in order to acquire data from the iCloud backup. However, this rendered the phone unable to backup recent data to iCloud, until the new iCloud password was entered. This however, requires the phone to be unlocked.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.latimes.com/business/la-fi-tn-apple-fbi-call-20160219-story.html|title=Apple and feds reveal San Bernardino shooter's iCloud password was reset hours after attack|work=Los Angeles Times|date=February 19, 2016|access-date=February 19, 2016|first=Paresh|last=Dave|archive-date=February 21, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160221034818/http://www.latimes.com/business/la-fi-tn-apple-fbi-call-20160219-story.html|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.yahoo.com/gma/san-bernardino-shooters-apple-id-passcode-changed-while-234003785--abc-news-topstories.html|title=San Bernardino Shooter's Apple ID Passcode Changed While in Government Possession, Apple Says|work=Yahoo! GMA|date=February 19, 2016|access-date=February 19, 2016|first=Jack|last=Date|archive-date=March 9, 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180309053127/https://www.yahoo.com/gma/san-bernardino-shooters-apple-id-passcode-changed-while-234003785--abc-news-topstories.html|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name=ReutersFeb20>{{cite news|last1=Volz|first1=Dustin|last2=Edwards|first2=Julia|title=U.S., Apple ratchet up rhetoric in fight over encryption|url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-apple-encryption-doj-idUSKCN0VS2FT|work=Reuters|date=February 20, 2016|access-date=February 20, 2016|archive-date=February 19, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160219231104/http://www.reuters.com/article/us-apple-encryption-doj-idUSKCN0VS2FT|url-status=live}}</ref> This was confirmed by the U.S. Department of Justice, which then added that any backup would have been "insufficient" because they would not have been able to recover enough information from it.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://ktla.com/2016/02/20/apple-says-law-enforcement-missed-chance-to-back-up-san-bernardino-shooters-iphone|title=Apple Says Law Enforcement Missed Chance to Back Up San Bernardino Shooter's iPhone|work=CNN Wire|date=February 20, 2016|access-date=February 20, 2016|archive-date=February 21, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160221090353/http://ktla.com/2016/02/20/apple-says-law-enforcement-missed-chance-to-back-up-san-bernardino-shooters-iphone/|url-status=live}}</ref>

=== Legal arguments ===
The government cited as precedent ''[[United States v. New York Telephone Co.]]'', in which the [[Supreme Court of the United States|Supreme Court]] ruled in 1977 that the All Writs Act gave courts the power to demand reasonable technical assistance from the phone company in accessing phone calling records. Apple responded that New York Telephone was already collecting the data in question in the course of its business, something the Supreme Court took note of in its ruling. Apple also asserts that being compelled to write new software "amounts to compelled speech and [[viewpoint discrimination]] in violation of the [[First Amendment to the United States Constitution|First Amendment]]. ... What is to stop the government from demanding that Apple [[Code as speech|write code]] to turn on the microphone in aid of government surveillance, activate the video camera, surreptitiously record conversations, or turn on location services to track the phone's user?" Apple argued that the FBI had not made use of all of the government's tools, such as employing the resources of the NSA. A hearing on the case was scheduled for March 22, 2016.<ref name=wired216>{{cite web|url=https://www.wired.com/2016/02/apple-brief-fbi-response-iphone/|title=Apple to FBI: You Can't Force Us to Hack the San Bernardino iPhone|first1=Kim|last1=Zetter|first2=Brian|last2=Barrett|magazine=Wired|date=February 25, 2016|access-date=February 25, 2016|archive-date=February 10, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210210092014/https://www.wired.com/2016/02/apple-brief-fbi-response-iphone/|url-status=live}}</ref>

San Bernardino County District Attorney [[Michael A. Ramos|Michael Ramos]] filed a brief stating the iPhone may contain evidence of a "lying dormant cyber pathogen" that could have been introduced into the San Bernardino County computer network,<ref>{{cite web|last1=Fagan|first1=Gary|title=In the Matter of the Search of an Apple iPhone Seized During the Execution of a Search Warrant on a Black Lexus IS300, California License Plate 35KGD203|url=https://arstechnica.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/sanbernardo.pdf|work=Ars Tecnica|date=March 4, 2016|access-date=March 10, 2016|archive-date=February 10, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210210091945/https://cdn.arstechnica.net/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/sanbernardo.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite news | first = David | last = Kravets | title = San Bernardino DA says seized iPhone may hold "dormant cyber pathogen" | url = https://arstechnica.com/tech-policy/2016/03/san-bernardino-da-says-seized-iphone-may-hold-dormant-cyber-pathogen/ | work = Ars Technica | date = March 3, 2016 | access-date = March 4, 2016 | quote = The iPhone is a county owned telephone that may have connected to the San Bernardino County computer network. The seized iPhone may contain evidence that can only be found on the seized phone that it was used as a weapon to introduce a lying dormant cyber pathogen that endangers San Bernardino's infrastructure. | archive-date = March 5, 2016 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20160305023142/http://arstechnica.com/tech-policy/2016/03/san-bernardino-da-says-seized-iphone-may-hold-dormant-cyber-pathogen/ | url-status = live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.pressenterprise.com/2016/03/04/san-bernardino-shooting-da-fears-terrorists-iphone-could-have-launched-cyber-attack/|title=SAN BERNARDINO SHOOTING: DA fears terrorist's iPhone could have launched cyber attack|work=The Press-Enterprise|date=March 4, 2016|access-date=March 5, 2016|first=David|last=Downey|archive-date=March 6, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160306110731/http://www.pe.com/articles/san-796176-bernardino-launced.html|url-status=live}}</ref> as well as identification of a possible third gunman who was alleged to have been seen at the scene of the attack by eyewitnesses.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.cbsnews.com/news/san-bernardino-shooting-prosecutor-iphone-could-id-unknown-attacker/|title=Prosecutor: iPhone could ID unknown San Bernardino attacker|work=CBS News|agency=Associated Press|date=March 4, 2016|access-date=March 5, 2016|archive-date=February 10, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210210092012/https://www.cbsnews.com/news/san-bernardino-shooting-prosecutor-iphone-could-id-unknown-attacker/|url-status=live}}</ref> The following day, Ramos told the [[Associated Press]] that he did not know whether the shooters had compromised the county's infrastructure, but the only way to know for sure was by gaining access to the iPhone.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Bailey |first1=Brandon |title=Does an extremist's iPhone contain a "cyber pathogen"? |url=http://hosted.ap.org/dynamic/stories/U/US_TEC_APPLE_IPHONE_PATHOGEN?SITE=TXWIC&SECTION=HOME&TEMPLATE=DEFAULT |agency=Associated Press |date=March 3, 2016 |access-date=March 10, 2016 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160310183553/http://hosted.ap.org/dynamic/stories/U/US_TEC_APPLE_IPHONE_PATHOGEN?SITE=TXWIC&SECTION=HOME&TEMPLATE=DEFAULT |archive-date=March 10, 2016 |df=mdy }}</ref><ref name="ars2">{{cite news|last1=Kravets|first1=David|title=What is a "lying-dormant cyber pathogen?" San Bernardino DA says it's made up [Update]|url=https://arstechnica.com/tech-policy/2016/03/what-is-a-lying-dormant-cyber-pathogen-san-bernardino-da-wont-say/|access-date=March 5, 2016|publisher=Ars Technica|date=March 4, 2016|quote=Did he use the county's infrastructure? Did he hack into that infrastructure? I don't know. In order for me to really put that issue to rest, there is one piece of evidence that would absolutely let us know that, and that would be the iPhone.|archive-date=February 10, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210210092024/https://arstechnica.com/tech-policy/2016/03/what-is-a-lying-dormant-cyber-pathogen-san-bernardino-da-wont-say/|url-status=live}}</ref> This statement has been criticized by cyber-security professionals as being improbable.<ref name="ars2" /><ref>{{cite news|last1=Collins|first1=Katie|title=Harry Potter fiction or iPhone weaponry? The 'dormant cyber pathogen' at the heart of Apple vs. FBI|url=http://www.cnet.com/news/apple-vs-fbi-harry-potter-iphone-dormant-cyber-pathogen/|access-date=March 5, 2016|publisher=[[CNET]]|date=March 4, 2016|archive-date=February 10, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210210092015/https://www.cnet.com/news/apple-vs-fbi-harry-potter-iphone-dormant-cyber-pathogen/|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=What's a 'cyber pathogen'? San Bernardino DA baffles security community|url=https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2016/mar/04/san-bernardino-da-baffles-security-community-lying-dormant-cyber-pathogen-iphone|access-date=March 5, 2016|work=The Guardian|date=March 4, 2016|archive-date=February 10, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210210092029/https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2016/mar/04/san-bernardino-da-baffles-security-community-lying-dormant-cyber-pathogen-iphone|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last1=Russel|first1=Jon|title=San Bernardino DA claims Syed Farouk's iPhone may house 'cyber pathogen'|url=https://techcrunch.com/2016/03/03/san-bernardino-da-claims-syed-farouks-iphone-may-house-cyber-pathogen/|access-date=March 5, 2016|publisher=[[Tech Crunch]]|date=March 4, 2016|archive-date=February 10, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210210092029/https://techcrunch.com/2016/03/03/san-bernardino-da-claims-syed-farouks-iphone-may-house-cyber-pathogen/|url-status=live}}</ref>

== Tim Cook's statements==
In an interview for a ''[[Time (magazine)|Time]]'' magazine cover story, Cook said that the issue is not "privacy versus security ... it's privacy and security or privacy and safety versus security." Cook also said, "[T]his is the golden age of surveillance that we live in. There is more information about all of us, so much more than ten years ago, or five years ago. It's everywhere. You are leaving digital footprints everywhere."<ref>{{cite magazine|url=https://time.com/4261796/tim-cook-transcript/|title=Transcript of Nancy Gibbs' interview with Tim Cook|magazine=Time|date=March 18, 2016|access-date=March 18, 2016|archive-date=February 10, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210210092211/https://time.com/4261796/tim-cook-transcript/|url-status=live}}</ref>

In a March 21, 2016, Apple press conference, Cook talked about the ongoing conflict with the FBI, saying, "[W]e have a responsibility to protect your data and your privacy. We will not shrink from this responsibility."<ref>{{cite web|url=https://techcrunch.com/2016/03/21/apples-tim-cook-on-iphone-unlocking-case-we-will-not-shrink-from-this-responsibility/|title=Apple's Tim Cook on iPhone unlocking case: 'We will not shrink from this responsibility'|date=March 21, 2016|publisher=AOL|agency=TechCrunch|access-date=March 21, 2016|archive-date=February 10, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210210092029/https://techcrunch.com/2016/03/21/apples-tim-cook-on-iphone-unlocking-case-we-will-not-shrink-from-this-responsibility/|url-status=live}}</ref>

=== FBI withdrawal of request ===
On March 21, 2016, the government requested and was granted a delay, saying a third party had demonstrated a possible way to unlock the iPhone in question and the FBI needed more time to determine if it will work.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://finance.yahoo.com/news/latest-fbi-may-found-way-230554970.html|title=The Latest: FBI, Apple hearing over unlocking phone canceled|publisher=Yahoo! News|agency=Associated Press|date=March 21, 2016|access-date=March 21, 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.cbsnews.com/news/fbi-may-have-found-way-to-unlock-san-bernardino-shooters-iphone/|title=FBI may have found way to unlock San Bernardino shooter's iPhone|work=CBS News|agency=Associated Press|date=March 21, 2016|access-date=March 22, 2016|archive-date=March 25, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160325150230/http://www.cbsnews.com/news/fbi-may-have-found-way-to-unlock-san-bernardino-shooters-iphone/|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.pressenterprise.com/2016/03/23/san-bernardino-shooting-israeli-company-is-helping-the-fbi-reports-say-update/|title=SAN BERNARDINO SHOOTING: Israeli company is helping the FBI, reports say|work=The Press-Enterprise|date=March 23, 2016|access-date=March 23, 2016|archive-date=March 24, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160324171813/http://www.pe.com/articles/company-797859-fbi-israeli.html|url-status=live}}</ref> On March 28, 2016, the FBI said it had unlocked the iPhone with the third party's help, and an anonymous official said that the hack's applications were limited; the Department of Justice withdrew the case.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://money.cnn.com/2016/03/28/news/companies/fbi-apple-iphone-case-cracked/index.html|title=FBI says it has cracked terrorist's iPhone without Apple's help|work=CNN Money|date=March 28, 2016|access-date=March 28, 2016|archive-date=February 10, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210210092016/https://money.cnn.com/2016/03/28/news/companies/fbi-apple-iphone-case-cracked/index.html|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://abcnews.go.com/Technology/justice-department-withdraws-request-apple-iphone-encryption-case/story?id=37986428|title=Justice Department Withdraws Request in Apple iPhone Encryption Case After FBI Accesses San Bernardino Shooter's Phone|work=[[ABC News (United States)|ABC News]]|first1=Jack|last1=Dale|first2=Mike|last2=Levine|first3=Alyssa|last3=Newcomb|date=March 28, 2016|access-date=March 28, 2016|archive-date=February 10, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210210092212/https://abcnews.go.com/Technology/justice-department-withdraws-request-apple-iphone-encryption-case/story?id=37986428|url-status=live}}</ref> The lawyer for the FBI claimed that they were using the alleged extracted information to further investigate the case.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2016/04/06/technology/fbi-lawyer-wont-say-if-data-from-unlocked-iphone-is-useful.html|title=F.B.I. Lawyer Won't Say if Data From Unlocked iPhone Is Useful|work=[[The New York Times]]|first=Eric|last=Lichtblau|date=April 6, 2016|access-date=April 6, 2016|archive-date=February 10, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210210092032/https://www.nytimes.com/2016/04/06/technology/fbi-lawyer-wont-say-if-data-from-unlocked-iphone-is-useful.html?_r=0|url-status=live}}</ref>

On April 7, 2016, FBI Director [[James Comey]] said that the tool used could only unlock an iPhone 5C like that used by the San Bernardino shooter as well as older iPhone models lacking the [[Touch ID]] sensor. Comey also confirmed that the tool was purchased from a third party but would not reveal the source,<ref>{{cite web|first=Samuel|last=Gibbs|date=April 7, 2016|url=https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2016/apr/07/san-bernardino-iphone-hack-work-newer-models-fbi-james-comey|title=San Bernardino iPhone hack won't work on newer models, says FBI|work=The Guardian|access-date=April 7, 2016|archive-date=February 10, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210210092031/https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2016/apr/07/san-bernardino-iphone-hack-work-newer-models-fbi-james-comey|url-status=live}}</ref> later indicating the tool cost more than $1.3 million and that they did not purchase the rights to technical details about how the tool functions.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2016/04/22/us/politics/fbi-director-suggests-bill-for-iphone-hacking-was-1-3-million.html|title=F.B.I. Director Suggests Bill for iPhone Hacking Topped $1.3 Million|first1=Eric|last1=Lichtblau|first2=Katie|last2=Benner|work=The New York Times|date=April 21, 2016|access-date=April 25, 2016|quote=Comey said the cost was 'more than I will make in the remainder of this job, which is 7 years and 4 months.'|archive-date=February 10, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210210092233/https://www.nytimes.com/2016/04/22/us/politics/fbi-director-suggests-bill-for-iphone-hacking-was-1-3-million.html|url-status=live}}</ref> Although the FBI claimed they were able to use other technological means to access the cellphone data from the San Bernardino shooter's iPhone 5C, without the aid of Apple, law enforcement still expresses concern over the encryption controversy.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|url=http://www.dailypress.com/news/crime/dp-nws-phone-encryption-20150412-story.html|title=Law enforcement worries over beefed-up phone encryption|last=Dujardin|first=Peter|date=April 12, 2015|website=Daily Press|access-date=May 2, 2016|archive-date=February 10, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210210092019/https://www.dailypress.com/news/crime/dp-nws-phone-encryption-20150412-story.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

Some news outlets, citing anonymous sources, identified the third party as Israeli company [[Cellebrite]]. However, ''The Washington Post'' reported that, according to anonymous "people familiar with the matter", the FBI had instead paid "professional hackers" who used a [[Zero-day (computing)|zero-day]] vulnerability in the iPhone's software to bypass its ten-try limitation, and did not need Cellebrite's assistance.<ref>{{cite news|first=Ellen|last=Nakashima|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/world/national-security/fbi-paid-professional-hackers-one-time-fee-to-crack-san-bernardino-iphone/2016/04/12/5397814a-00de-11e6-9d36-33d198ea26c5_story.html|title=FBI paid professional hackers one-time fee to crack San Bernardino iPhone|newspaper=The Washington Post|date=April 12, 2016|access-date=April 14, 2016|archive-date=April 14, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160414134313/https://www.washingtonpost.com/world/national-security/fbi-paid-professional-hackers-one-time-fee-to-crack-san-bernardino-iphone/2016/04/12/5397814a-00de-11e6-9d36-33d198ea26c5_story.html|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.mbgadget.com/2016/03/government-keeping-his-technique-to.html|title=Government keeping his technique to crack San Bernardino iPhone 'classified'|website=www.mbgadget.com|access-date=2016-12-02|archive-date=February 2, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170202141742/http://www.mbgadget.com/2016/03/government-keeping-his-technique-to.html}}</ref> In April 2021, ''The Washington Post'' reported that the Australian company Azimuth Security, a [[White hat (computer security)|white hat]] hacking firm, had been the one to help the FBI, with work from security researchers [[Mark Dowd]] and [[David Wang (hacker)|David Wang]].<ref>{{Cite news|last1=Nakashima|first1=Ellen|last2=Albergotti|first2=Reed|date=April 14, 2021|title=The FBI wanted to unlock the San Bernardino shooter's iPhone. It turned to a little-known Australian firm.|newspaper=[[The Washington Post]]|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/technology/2021/04/14/azimuth-san-bernardino-apple-iphone-fbi/|access-date=April 15, 2021}}</ref> In 2020, the New York Times reported that "new data reveals a twist to the encryption debate that undercuts both sides," with public records showing that at least 2,000 US law enforcement agencies had since acquired "tools to get into locked, encrypted phones and extract their data," mostly from Cellebrite and [[Grayshift]].<ref>{{Cite news |last=Nicas |first=Jack |date=2020-10-21 |title=The Police Can Probably Break Into Your Phone |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2020/10/21/technology/iphone-encryption-police.html |access-date=2024-07-17 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref>

== Other All Writs Act cases involving iPhones ==
[[File:State-by-state usage of the All Writs Act on Apple and Google.svg|thumb|right|State-by-state usage of the All Writs Act by the [[federal government of the United States]] against Apple Inc. and Google:<ref>{{cite web|last1=Pagliery|first1=Jose|title=Here are the places feds are using a controversial law to unlock phones|url=https://money.cnn.com/2016/03/30/technology/phones-all-writs-act/index.html?sr=twmoney050116phones-all-writs-act0531AMStoryLink&linkId=23917662|website=[[CNN]]|publisher=[[Time Warner]]|access-date=April 30, 2016|date=March 30, 2016|archive-date=February 10, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210210092021/https://money.cnn.com/2016/03/30/technology/phones-all-writs-act/index.html?sr=twmoney050116phones-all-writs-act0531AMStoryLink&linkId=23917662|url-status=dead}}</ref>
