York]] in Brooklyn (''In re Order Requiring Apple Inc. to Assist in the Execution of a Search Warrant Issued by the Court'', case number 1:15-mc-01902<ref name="MemOrder" />), after the [[Magistrate|magistrate judge]] in the case, James Orenstein, requested Apple's position before issuing an order.<ref>{{cite web|first=Emily|last=Field|url=http://www.law360.com/articles/718821/apple-says-gov-t-can-t-force-it-to-unlock-iphone|title=Apple Says Gov't Can't Force It To Unlock iPhone|work=[[Law360]]|access-date=March 3, 2016|archive-date=February 10, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210210092239/https://www.law360.com/articles/718821/apple-says-gov-t-can-t-force-it-to-unlock-iphone|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.ft.com/content/c811f652-dade-11e5-98fd-06d75973fe09|title=Apple's legal strategy v FBI has roots in case heard last year|first1=Tim|last1=Bradshaw|first2=Richard|last2=Waters|work=[[Financial Times]]|date=February 24, 2016|access-date=February 25, 2016|archive-date=February 10, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210210092028/https://www.ft.com/content/c811f652-dade-11e5-98fd-06d75973fe09|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://blogs.reuters.com/alison-frankel/2016/02/17/how-a-n-y-judge-inspired-apples-encryption-fight-with-justice/|title=How a N.Y. judge inspired Apple's encryption fight with Justice|first=Alison|last=Frankel|work=Reuters|date=February 17, 2016|access-date=March 11, 2016|archive-date=March 12, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160312121720/http://blogs.reuters.com/alison-frankel/2016/02/17/how-a-n-y-judge-inspired-apples-encryption-fight-with-justice/|url-status=dead}}</ref> On February 29, 2016, Judge Orenstein denied the government's request, saying the All Writs Act cannot be used to force a company to modify its products: "The implications of the government's position are so far-reaching – both in terms of what it would allow today and what it implies about Congressional intent in 1789 – as to produce impermissibly absurd results."<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2016/feb/29/apple-fbi-case-drug-dealer-iphone-jun-feng-san-bernardino|title=Apple case: judge rejects FBI request for access to drug dealer's iPhone|first1=Spencer|last1=Ackerman|first2=Sam|last2=Thielman|first3=Danny|last3=Yadron|work=The Guardian|date=February 29, 2016|access-date=February 29, 2016|archive-date=February 10, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210210092028/https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2016/feb/29/apple-fbi-case-drug-dealer-iphone-jun-feng-san-bernardino|url-status=live}}</ref> Orenstein went on to criticize the government's stance, writing, "It would be absurd to posit that the authority the government sought was anything other than obnoxious to the law."<ref name="MemOrder">[https://www.documentcloud.org/documents/2728314-Orenstein-Order.html In Re Order requiring Apple, Inc. to assist in the execution of a search warrant issued by the court, Memorandum and Order] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210210092215/https://www.documentcloud.org/documents/2728314-Orenstein-Order.html |date=February 10, 2021 }}, James Orenstein, Magistrate Judge, U.S. District Court, Eastern District of New York (Brooklyn), 1:15-mc-1902 (JO), February 29, 2016</ref><ref name="Smythe1" /><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2016-02-29/apple-wins-in-brooklyn-battle-over-unlocking-iphone|title=Apple Wins in Brooklyn Battle Over Unlocking iPhone|first1=Christie|last1=Smythe|first2=Tiffany|last2=Kary|work=Bloomberg News|date=February 29, 2016|access-date=March 2, 2016}}</ref> The Justice Department appealed the ruling to District Court Judge Margot Brodie.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://news.yahoo.com/justice-department-asks-judge-revisit-ny-iphone-case-011447599--finance.html|title=Justice Department asks judge to revisit NY iPhone case|first=Julia|last=Edwards|agency=Reuters|publisher=Yahoo! News|date=March 7, 2016|access-date=March 8, 2016|archive-date=February 10, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210210092044/https://news.yahoo.com/justice-department-asks-judge-revisit-ny-iphone-case-011447599--finance.html|url-status=live}}</ref> Apple requested a delay while the FBI attempted to access the San Bernardino iPhone without Apple's help.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://finance.yahoo.com/news/citing-fbi-quest-apple-asks-145752747.html|title=Citing FBI quest, Apple asks judge to delay iPhone data case|publisher=Yahoo! News|agency=Associated Press|date=March 25, 2016|access-date=March 25, 2016}}</ref> On April 8, after the FBI succeeded, the Justice Department told the Brooklyn court it intended to press forward with its demand for assistance there,<ref>{{cite web|url=https://finance.yahoo.com/news/u-continue-appeal-iphone-data-151043351.html|title=U.S. to continue appeal of iPhone data case in New York|publisher=Yahoo! Finance|agency=Reuters|date=April 8, 2016|access-date=April 8, 2016|archive-date=February 10, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210210092049/https://finance.yahoo.com/news/u-continue-appeal-iphone-data-151043351.html|url-status=live}}</ref> but on April 22, the government withdrew its request, telling the court "an individual" (the suspect, according to press reports) had provided the correct passcode.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.ft.com/intl/cms/s/0/d1090a5c-0905-11e6-b6d3-746f8e9cdd33.html#axzz46q2skSK8|title=FBI ends stand-off with Apple over iPhone|first=Tim|last=Bradshaw|work=FT|date=April 23, 2016|access-date=April 25, 2016|archive-date=February 10, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210210092244/https://www.ft.com/content/d1090a5c-0905-11e6-b6d3-746f8e9cdd33#axzz46q2skSK8|url-status=live}}</ref>

== Reactions ==
National reactions to Apple's opposition of the order were mixed.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.cnn.com/2016/02/18/us/san-bernardino-shooter-phone-apple-reaction|title=Anger, praise for Apple for rebuffing FBI over San Bernardino killer's phone|publisher=CNN|date=February 18, 2016|access-date=February 19, 2016|first1=Greg|last1=Botelho|first2=Lorenza|last2=Brascia|first3=Michael|last3=Martinez|archive-date=February 19, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160219103313/http://www.cnn.com/2016/02/18/us/san-bernardino-shooter-phone-apple-reaction/|url-status=live}}</ref> A [[CBS News]] poll that sampled 1,022 Americans found that 50% of the respondents supported the FBI's stance, while 45% supported Apple's stance.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.cbsnews.com/news/cbs-news-poll-americans-split-on-unlocking-san-bernardino-shooters-iphone/|title=CBS News poll: Americans split on unlocking San Bernardino shooter's iPhone|work=CBS News|date=March 18, 2016|access-date=March 19, 2016|archive-date=March 20, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160320032136/http://www.cbsnews.com/news/cbs-news-poll-americans-split-on-unlocking-san-bernardino-shooters-iphone/|url-status=live}}</ref> Also, 1,002 surveyed Americans who own smartphones were divided into two sides; 51% were against Apple's decision, while 38% supported their stance.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.people-press.org/2016/02/22/more-support-for-justice-department-than-for-apple-in-dispute-over-unlocking-iphone/|title=More Support for Justice Department Than for Apple in Dispute Over Unlocking iPhone|website=Pew Research Center for the People and the Press|date=February 22, 2016 |access-date=April 24, 2016|archive-date=February 10, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210210092227/https://www.pewresearch.org/politics/2016/02/22/more-support-for-justice-department-than-for-apple-in-dispute-over-unlocking-iphone/|url-status=live}}</ref>

=== Support for Apple ===
The [[Reform Government Surveillance]] coalition, which includes major tech firms like [[Google]], [[Microsoft]], [[Facebook]], [[Yahoo!]], [[Twitter]], and [[LinkedIn]], has indicated its opposition to the order.<ref>{{cite news|title=Reform Government Surveillance Statement Regarding Encryption and Security|url=http://reformgs.tumblr.com/post/139513553507/reform-government-surveillance-statement|agency=[[Reform Government Surveillance]]|date=February 17, 2016|access-date=February 24, 2016|archive-date=February 10, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210210092216/https://reformgs.tumblr.com/post/139513553507/reform-government-surveillance-statement|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last1=Clark|first1=Jack|title=Google, Tech Companies Side With Apple in Decryption Protest|url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2016-02-18/google-sides-with-apple-in-protesting-government-decryption|access-date=February 24, 2016|publisher=[[Bloomberg L.P.|Bloomberg]]|date=February 17, 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last1=Andor Brodeur|first1=Michael|title=FBI v. Apple: What's at stake in encryption fight|url=https://www.bostonglobe.com/arts/2016/02/23/fbi-apple-what-stake-encryption-fight/cYlBxyhfMIrzU3EvnAqIaI/story.html|access-date=February 23, 2016|newspaper=The Boston Globe|date=February 23, 2016|archive-date=February 10, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210210092049/https://www.bostonglobe.com/arts/2016/02/23/fbi-apple-what-stake-encryption-fight/cYlBxyhfMIrzU3EvnAqIaI/story.html|url-status=live}}</ref> By March 3, the deadline, a large number of ''[[amicus curiae]]'' briefs were filed with the court, with numerous technology firms supporting Apple's position, including a joint brief from [[Amazon.com]], [[Box (company)|Box]], [[Cisco Systems]], [[Dropbox (service)|Dropbox]], [[Evernote]], Facebook, [[Google]], [[Lavabit]], Microsoft, [[Mozilla]], [[Nest Labs]], [[Pinterest]], [[Slack Technologies]], [[Snapchat]], [[WhatsApp]], and Yahoo!. Briefs from the [[American Civil Liberties Union]], the [[Electronic Frontier Foundation]], Access Now, and the Center for Democracy and Technology also supported Apple.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.theverge.com/2016/3/3/11156704/apple-fbi-amicus-briefs-iphone-encryption-fight|title=Google, Microsoft, and other tech giants file legal briefs in support of Apple|first=Russell|last=Brandom|work=The Verge|date=March 3, 2016|access-date=March 4, 2016|archive-date=February 10, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210210092051/https://www.theverge.com/2016/3/3/11156704/apple-fbi-amicus-briefs-iphone-encryption-fight|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://cdn3.vox-cdn.com/uploads/chorus_asset/file/6141865/appleBriefasfiled__1___1_.0.pdf|title=Brief of Amici Curiae Amazon, et al.|first1=Michael|last1=Maddigan|first2=Neil|last2=Katyal|work=Hogan Lovells US LLP|date=March 2, 2016|access-date=March 4, 2016|archive-date=February 10, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210210092005/https://cdn3.vox-cdn.com/uploads/chorus_asset/file/6141865/appleBriefasfiled__1___1_.0.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url = https://www.apple.com/pr/library/2016/03/03Amicus-Briefs-in-Support-of-Apple.html|title = Amicus Briefs in Support of Apple|date = March 3, 2016|access-date = March 4, 2016|publisher = Apple Press Info|archive-date = February 10, 2021|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20210210092249/https://www.apple.com/newsroom/|url-status = live}}</ref>

The [[think tank]] [[Niskanen Center]] has suggested that the case is a [[door-in-the-face technique]] designed to gain eventual approval for [[encryption]] [[Backdoor (computing)|backdoors]]<ref name="Intercept1">{{cite news|last1=Froomkin|first1=Dan|last2=McLaughlin|first2=Jenna|title=FBI vs. Apple Establishes a New Phase of the Crypto Wars|url=https://theintercept.com/2016/02/26/fbi-vs-apple-post-crypto-wars/|access-date=February 26, 2016|publisher=[[The Intercept]]|date=February 26, 2016}}</ref> and is viewed as a revival of the [[Crypto Wars]].<ref name="Newsweek1">{{cite news|last1=Lee|first1=Sung|title=The government's decades-long battle for backdoors in encryption|url=http://www.newsweek.com/governments-decades-long-battle-backdoors-encryption-430868|access-date=February 27, 2016|magazine=[[Newsweek]]|date=February 26, 2016|archive-date=February 10, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210210092120/https://www.newsweek.com/governments-decades-long-battle-backdoors-encryption-430868|url-status=live}}</ref>

U.S. Representative [[Mike Honda]], a Democrat who represented the [[Silicon Valley]] region, voiced his support for Apple.<ref name=theguardian20160227/>

On February 23, 2016, a series of pro-Apple protests organized by [[Fight for the Future]] were held outside of Apple's stores in over 40 locations.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Reisinger|first1=Don|title=Will You Protest the FBI at Apple Stores on Tuesday?|url=http://fortune.com/2016/02/22/apple-stores-protests/|access-date=March 13, 2016|publisher=[[Fortune (magazine)|Fortune]]|date=February 22, 2016|archive-date=February 10, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210210092120/https://fortune.com/2016/02/22/apple-stores-protests/|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last1=MOSCARITOLO|first1=ANGELA|title=Protesters Gather to Support Apple in FBI iPhone Fight|url=https://www.pcmag.com/article2/0,2817,2499909,00.asp|access-date=March 13, 2016|publisher=[[PCMag]]|date=February 24, 2016|archive-date=February 10, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210210092125/https://www.pcmag.com/news/photos-protesters-gather-to-support-apple-in-fbi-iphone-fight|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last1=CUTHBERTSON|first1=ANTHONY|title=APPLE STORE PROTESTS OVER ENCRYPTION BATTLE PLANNED WORLDWIDE|url=http://www.newsweek.com/apple-store-protests-planned-across-us-over-encryption-428948|access-date=March 13, 2016|work=[[Newsweek]]|date=February 22, 2016|archive-date=February 10, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210210092221/https://www.newsweek.com/apple-store-protests-planned-across-us-over-encryption-428948|url-status=live}}</ref>

[[Prince Zeid bin Ra'ad|Zeid Ra'ad al-Hussein]], the [[Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights|United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights]], warned the FBI of the potential for "extremely damaging implications" on [[human rights]] and that they "risk unlocking a [[Pandora's box]]" through their investigation.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.pressenterprise.com/2016/03/04/san-bernardino-shooting-un-chief-warns-of-implications-of-apple-fbi-row/|title=San Bernardino Shooting: UN chief warns of implications of Apple-FBI row|publisher=The Press-Enterprise|agency=Associated Press|date=March 4, 2016|access-date=March 4, 2016|archive-date=February 10, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210210092057/https://www.pe.com/2016/03/04/san-bernardino-shooting-un-chief-warns-of-implications-of-apple-fbi-row/|url-status=live}}</ref>

General [[Michael Hayden (general)|Michael Hayden]], former director of the NSA and the [[Central Intelligence Agency]], in a March 7 interview with [[Maria Bartiromo]] on the [[Fox Business Network]], supported Apple's position, noting that the CIA considers [[cyber-attack]]s the number one threat to U.S. security and saying that "this may be a case where we've got to give up some things in law enforcement and even counter terrorism in order to preserve this aspect, our cybersecurity."<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.foxbusiness.com/features/2016/03/07/fmr-nsa-cia-chief-hayden-sides-with-apple-over-feds.html|title=Fmr. NSA, CIA Chief Hayden Sides with Apple Over Feds|first=Julia|last=Limitone|work=Fox Business|date=March 7, 2016|access-date=March 9, 2016|archive-date=February 10, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210210092239/https://www.foxbusiness.com/features/fmr-nsa-cia-chief-hayden-sides-with-apple-over-feds|url-status=live}}</ref>

Salihin Kondoker, whose wife was shot in the attack but survived, filed a friend of the court brief siding with Apple; his brief said that he "understand[s] that this software the government wants them to use will be used against millions of other innocent people. I share their fear."<ref>{{cite web|url=https://techcrunch.com/2016/02/29/san-bernardino-survivors-husband-backs-apple-in-battle-with-fbi/|title=San Bernardino survivor's husband backs Apple in battle with FBI|date=February 29, 2016|publisher=AOL|agency=TechCrunch|access-date=March 21, 2016|archive-date=February 10, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210210092300/https://techcrunch.com/2016/02/29/san-bernardino-survivors-husband-backs-apple-in-battle-with-fbi/|url-status=live}}</ref>

[[Edward Snowden]] said that the FBI already has the technical means to unlock Apple's devices and said, "The global technological consensus is against the FBI."<ref>{{cite web|url=http://fortune.com/2016/03/09/snowden-fbi-apple-iphone/|title=Snowden: FBI Saying It Can't Unlock iPhone is 'Bullsh**'|first=Don|last=Reisinger|work=Fortune|date=March 9, 2016|access-date=March 9, 2016|archive-date=February 10, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210210092155/https://fortune.com/2016/03/09/snowden-fbi-apple-iphone/|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://twitter.com/Snowden/status/707299113449230336|title=The global technological consensus is against the FBI. Why? Here's one example|first=Edward|last=Snowden|work=Twitter|date=March 8, 2016|access-date=March 9, 2016|archive-date=February 10, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210210092246/https://twitter.com/Snowden/status/707299113449230336|url-status=live}}</ref>

[[McAfee]] founder and [[Libertarian Party (United States)|Libertarian Party]] [[Libertarian Party presidential primaries, 2016|presidential primary]] candidate [[John McAfee]] had publicly volunteered to decrypt the iPhone used by the San Bernardino shooters, avoiding the need for Apple to build a backdoor.<ref>{{cite web |last=Hathaway |first=Jay |title=Antivirus Wild Man John McAfee Offers to Solve FBI's iPhone Problem So Apple Doesn't Have To |url=http://nymag.com/following/2016/02/john-mcafee-says-he-can-crack-that-iphone.html |work=Following: How We Live Online |date=February 19, 2016 |access-date=February 24, 2016 |archive-date=February 23, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160223133848/http://nymag.com/following/2016/02/john-mcafee-says-he-can-crack-that-iphone.html |url-status=live }}</ref> He later indicated that the method he would employ, extracting the unique ID from inside the A7 processor chip, is difficult and risks permanently locking the phone, and that he was seeking publicity.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.dailydot.com/politics/john-mcafee-lied-iphone-apple-fbi/|title=John McAfee lied about San Bernardino shooter's iPhone hack to 'get a s**tload of public attention'|first=William|last=Turton|work=The Daily Dot|date=March 7, 2016|access-date=March 7, 2016|archive-date=May 15, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160515024010/http://www.dailydot.com/politics/john-mcafee-lied-iphone-apple-fbi/|url-status=live}}</ref>

[[Ron Wyden]], [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] senator for Oregon and a noted privacy and encryption advocate, questioned the FBI's honesty concerning the contents of the phone. He said in a statement, "There are real questions about whether [the FBI] has been straight with the public on [the Apple case]."<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.zdnet.com/article/fbis-strategy-in-apple-case-caught-in-distortion-field/|title=FBI's strategy in Apple case caught in distortion field|work=[[ZDNet]]|first=John|last=Fontana|date=April 6, 2016|access-date=April 6, 2016|archive-date=February 10, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210210092232/https://www.zdnet.com/article/fbis-strategy-in-apple-case-caught-in-distortion-field/|url-status=live}}</ref>

=== Support for FBI ===
Some families of the victims and survivors of the attack indicated they would file a brief in support of the FBI.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://abcnews.go.com/Technology/wireStory/basic-software-held-key-shooters-iphone-unused-37106947 |title=Some Victims in Terror Attack Support Efforts to Hack iPhone |first1=Tami |last1=Abdullah |first2=Amanda Lee |last2=Myers |agency=Associated Press |work=ABC News |date=February 22, 2016 |access-date=February 25, 2016 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160224120439/https://abcnews.go.com/Technology/wireStory/basic-software-held-key-shooters-iphone-unused-37106947 |archive-date=February 24, 2016 }}</ref>

The [[National Sheriffs' Association]] has suggested that Apple's stance is "putting profit over safety" and "has nothing to do with privacy."<ref name="Smythe1">{{cite news|last1=Smythe|first1=Christie|last2=Wang|first2=Selina|last3=Kary|first3=Tiffany|title=Apple Goes to Washington Fresh From Big Boost in iPhone Fight|url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2016-03-01/apple-goes-to-washington-with-some-wind-in-its-sails|access-date=March 1, 2016|publisher=[[Bloomberg L.P.|Bloomberg]]|date=March 1, 2016}}</ref> The [[Federal Law Enforcement Officers Association]], the [[Association of Prosecuting Attorneys]], and the National Sheriffs' Association filed a brief supporting the FBI.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Nelson|first1=Joe|title=State, federal law enforcement agencies file in support of FBI in Apple battle|date=March 3, 2016 |url=http://www.sbsun.com/technology/20160303/state-federal-law-enforcement-agencies-file-in-support-of-fbi-in-apple-battle|publisher=San Bernardino County Sun|access-date=March 30, 2016|archive-date=February 10, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210210092128/https://www.sbsun.com/2016/03/03/state-federal-law-enforcement-agencies-file-in-support-of-fbi-in-apple-battle/|url-status=live}}</ref>

"With Apple's privacy policy for the customers there is no way of getting into a phone without a person's master password. With this policy there will be no backdoor access on the phone for the law enforcement to access the person's private information. This has caused a great dispute between the FBI and Apple's encryption.<ref name=":1" /> Apple has closed this backdoor for the law enforcement because they believe that by creating this backdoor it would make it easier for law enforcement, and also make it easier for criminal hackers to gain access to people's personal data on their phone." Former FBI director [[James Comey]] says that "We are drifting to a place in this country where there will be zones that are beyond the reach of the law."<ref name=":1" /> He believes that this backdoor access is crucial to investigations, and without it many criminals will not be convicted.<ref name=":1" />

Senator [[Dianne Feinstein]] of [[California]], a Democrat and vice chairman of the [[Senate Intelligence Committee]], voiced her opposition to Apple.<ref name=theguardian20160227>{{cite web|last1=Thielman|first1=Sam|last2=Yadron|first2=Danny|title=Crunch time for Apple as it prepares for face-off with FBI|url=https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2016/feb/27/apple-fbi-congressional-hearing-iphone-encryption|newspaper=[[The Guardian]]|access-date=March 1, 2016|date=February 27, 2016|archive-date=February 10, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210210092053/https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2016/feb/27/apple-fbi-congressional-hearing-iphone-encryption|url-status=live}}</ref> All [[Republican Party presidential candidates, 2016|candidates for the Republican nomination]] for the [[2016 United States presidential election|2016 U.S. presidential election]] who had not dropped out of the race before February 19, 2016, supported the FBI's position, though several expressed concerns about adding backdoors to mobile phones.<ref name=20160219-25/>

On February 23, 2016, the ''[[Financial Times]]'' reported<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.ft.com/intl/cms/s/2/3559f46e-d9c5-11e5-98fd-06d75973fe09.html#axzz417MxjWob|title=Gates breaks ranks over FBI Apple request|first1=Stephen|last1=Foley|first2=Tim|last2=Bradshaw|work=Financial Times|date=February 23, 2016|access-date=February 25, 2016|archive-date=February 10, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210210092101/https://www.ft.com/content/3559f46e-d9c5-11e5-98fd-06d75973fe09#axzz417MxjWob|url-status=live}}</ref> that [[Bill Gates]], founder of Microsoft, has sided with the FBI in the case. However, Gates later said in an interview with [[Bloomberg News]] "that doesn't state my view on this."<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/videos/2016-02-23/gates-disputes-report-that-he-backs-fbi-in-apple-dispute|title=Gates disputes report that he backs FBI in Apple dispute|publisher=Bloomberg|date=February 23, 2016|access-date=February 25, 2016}}</ref> He added that he thought the right balance and safeguards need to be found in the courts and in Congress, and that the debate provoked by this case is valuable.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2016/02/24/technology/bill-gates-apple.html|title=Bill Gates Weighs In on Apple's Clash With the F.B.I.|first=Mike|last=McPhatefeb|work=The New York Times|date=February 23, 2016|access-date=February 25, 2016|archive-date=February 10, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210210092102/https://www.nytimes.com/2016/02/24/technology/bill-gates-apple.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

San Bernardino Police Chief Jarrod Burguan said in an interview:

{{blockquote|I'll be honest with you, I think that there is a reasonably good chance that there is nothing of any value on the phone. What we are hoping might be on the phone would be potential contacts that we would obviously want to talk to. This is an effort to leave no stone unturned in the investigation. [To] allow this phone to sit there and not make an effort to get the information or the data that may be inside of that phone is simply not fair to the victims and their families.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.npr.org/2016/02/26/468216198/san-bernardino-police-chief-weighs-in-on-whether-apple-should-unlock-shooter-s-p|title=San Bernardino Police Chief Sees Chance Nothing of Value On Shooter's iPhone|publisher=NPR|date=February 26, 2016|access-date=February 27, 2016|archive-date=February 10, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210210092103/https://www.npr.org/2016/02/26/468216198/san-bernardino-police-chief-weighs-in-on-whether-apple-should-unlock-shooter-s-p|url-status=live}}</ref>}}

[[Manhattan District Attorney]] [[Cyrus Vance Jr.]], said that he wants Apple to unlock 175 iPhones that his office's [[Cyber-Crime Lab]] has been unable to access, adding, "Apple should be directed to be able to unlock its phones when there is a court order by an independent judge proving and demonstrating that there's relevant evidence on that phone necessary for an individual case."<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.npr.org/2016/02/21/467547180/it-s-not-just-the-iphone-law-enforcement-wants-to-unlock|title=It's Not Just The iPhone Law Enforcement Wants To Unlock|publisher=NPR|date=February 21, 2016|access-date=March 3, 2016|archive-date=February 10, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210210092249/https://www.npr.org/2016/02/21/467547180/it-s-not-just-the-iphone-law-enforcement-wants-to-unlock|url-status=live}}</ref>

FBI Director Comey, testifying before the [[House Judiciary Committee]], compared Apple's iPhone security to a [[guard dog]], saying, "We're asking Apple to take the vicious guard dog away and let us [[Lockpicking|pick the lock]]."<ref>{{cite web|url=http://sanfrancisco.cbslocal.com/2016/03/01/apple-fbi-stake-out-competing-sides-in-encryption-debate|title=Apple clash before Congress as encryption fight simmers|first1=Tami|last1=Abdollah|first2=Larry|last2=Neumeister|work=CBS News|date=March 1, 2016|access-date=March 3, 2016|archive-date=February 10, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210210092245/https://sanfrancisco.cbslocal.com/2016/03/01/apple-fbi-stake-out-competing-sides-in-encryption-debate/|url-status=live}}</ref>

Apple's [[iOS 8]] and later have encryption mechanisms that make it difficult for the government to get through. Apple provided no backdoor for surveillance without the company's discretion. However, Comey stated that he did not want a backdoor method of surveillance and that "We want to use the front door, with clarity and transparency, and with clear guidance provided by law." He believes that special access is required in order to stop criminals such as "terrorists and child molesters".<ref name=":2">{{cite web|url=http://www.cnet.com/news/fbi-director-demands-access-to-private-cell-phone-data/|title=FBI director demands access to private cell phone data|last=Rosenblatt|first=Seth|date=October 16, 2014|work=CNET|access-date=May 2, 2016|archive-date=February 10, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210210092110/https://www.cnet.com/news/fbi-director-demands-access-to-private-cell-phone-data/|url-status=live}}</ref>

=== Calls for compromise ===
Both [[Democratic Party presidential candidates, 2016|2016 Democratic presidential candidates]]&mdash;former [[United States Secretary of State|Secretary of State]] [[Hillary Clinton]] and Senator [[Bernie Sanders]]&mdash;suggested some compromise should be found.<ref name=20160219-25>{{cite web |url=https://www.csmonitor.com/World/Passcode/2016/0219/What-presidential-candidates-are-saying-about-the-Apple-v.-FBI-debate |title=What presidential candidates are saying about the Apple v. FBI debate |work=The Christian Science Monitor |date=February 19, 2016 |access-date=February 25, 2016 |archive-date=February 10, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210210092109/https://www.csmonitor.com/World/Passcode/2016/0219/What-presidential-candidates-are-saying-about-the-Apple-v.-FBI-debate |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.yahoo.com/politics/every-republican-presidential-candidate-sides-with-044526788.html|title=Every GOP presidential candidate sides with the FBI in fight with Apple|first=Alyssa|last=Bereznak|work=Yahoo! News|date=February 25, 2016|access-date=February 25, 2016|archive-date=February 10, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210210092302/https://www.yahoo.com/news/every-republican-presidential-candidate-sides-with-044526788.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

[[United States Secretary of Defense|U.S. Defense Secretary]] [[Ashton Carter]] called for Silicon Valley and the federal government to work together. "We are squarely behind strong data security and strong encryption, no question about it," he said. Carter also added that he is "not a believer in back doors."<ref>{{cite web|url=http://fortune.com/2016/03/02/secretary-defense-encryption-back-doors/|title=Defense Secretary Says He Is For Encryption And Against Back Doors|work=Fortune|first=Jonathan|last=Vanian|date=March 2, 2016|access-date=March 3, 2016|archive-date=February 10, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210210092255/https://fortune.com/2016/03/02/secretary-defense-encryption-back-doors/|url-status=live}}</ref>

In an address to the 2016 [[South by Southwest]] conference on March 11, President [[Barack Obama]] stated that while he could not comment on the specific case, "You cannot take an absolutist view on [encryption]. If your view is strong encryption no matter what, and we can and should create black boxes, that does not strike the balance that we've lived with for 200 or 300 years. And it's fetishizing our phones above every other value. That can't be the right answer."<ref name="Machkovech1">{{cite news|last1=Machkovech|first1=Sam|title=Obama weighs in on Apple v. FBI: "You can't take an absolutist view"|url=https://arstechnica.com/tech-policy/2016/03/obama-weighs-in-on-apple-v-fbi-you-cant-take-an-absolutist-view/|access-date=March 12, 2016|publisher=Ars Technica|date=March 11, 2016|archive-date=February 10, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210210092109/https://arstechnica.com/tech-policy/2016/03/obama-weighs-in-on-apple-v-fbi-you-cant-take-an-absolutist-view/|url-status=live}}</ref>

=== Proposed legislation ===
On April 13, 2016, U.S. Senators [[Richard Burr]] and [[Dianne Feinstein]], the Republican Chair and senior Democrat on the [[Senate Intelligence Committee]], respectively, released draft legislation that would authorize state and federal judges to order "any person who provides a product or method to facilitate a communication or the processing or storage of data" to provide data in intelligible form or technical assistance in unlocking encrypted data and that any such person who distributes software or devices must ensure they are capable of complying with such an order.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-apple-encryption-legislation-idUSKCN0X52CG|title=Leak of Senate encryption bill prompts swift backlash|first1=Dustin|last1=Volz|first2=Mark|last2=Hosenball|work=Reuters|date=April 8, 2016|access-date=April 14, 2016|archive-date=February 10, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210210092205/https://www.reuters.com/article/us-apple-encryption-legislation-idUSKCN0X52CG|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://finance.yahoo.com/news/u-senate-panel-releases-draft-192224282.html|title=U.S. Senate panel releases draft of controversial encryption bill|first1=Mark|last1=Hosenball|first2=Dustin|last2=Volz|publisher=Yahoo! Finance|agency=Reuters|date=April 13, 2016|access-date=April 14, 2016|archive-date=February 10, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210210092057/https://finance.yahoo.com/news/u-senate-panel-releases-draft-192224282.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

===Freedom of Information Act lawsuit===
In September 2016, the [[Associated Press]], [[Vice Media]], and [[Gannett Company|Gannett]] (the owner of ''[[USA Today]]'') filed a [[Freedom of Information Act (United States)|Freedom of Information Act]] (FOIA) lawsuit against the FBI, seeking to compel the agency to reveal who it hired to unlock Farook's iPhone, and how much was paid.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/nation/2016/09/16/usa-today-lawsuit-fbi-iphone-hack-san-bernardino/90477540/|title=USA Today, others sue FBI for info on phone hack of San Bernardino shooter|work=USA Today|date=September 16, 2016|access-date=September 17, 2016|first=Brad|last=Heath|archive-date=September 17, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160917012058/http://www.usatoday.com/story/news/nation/2016/09/16/usa-today-lawsuit-fbi-iphone-hack-san-bernardino/90477540/|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="GersteinFOIA">Josh Gerstein, [https://www.politico.com/blogs/under-the-radar/2017/10/01/judge-fbi-need-not-release-cost-of-iphone-hack-243338 Judge: FBI can keep cost of iPhone hack secret] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171029083803/https://www.politico.com/blogs/under-the-radar/2017/10/01/judge-fbi-need-not-release-cost-of-iphone-hack-243338 |date=October 29, 2017 }}, ''Politico'' (October 1, 2017).</ref> On September 30, 2017, a federal court ruled against the media organizations and granted [[summary judgment]] in the government's favor.<ref name="GersteinFOIA"/><ref>''[https://ecf.dcd.uscourts.gov/cgi-bin/show_public_doc?2016cv1850-22 Associated Press v. Federal Bureau of Investigation] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190420090447/https://ecf.dcd.uscourts.gov/cgi-bin/show_public_doc?2016cv1850-22 |date=April 20, 2019 }}'', Civil Action No. 16-cv-1850 (TSC) (D.D.C. Sept. 13, 2017).</ref> The court ruled that the company that hacked the iPhone and the amount paid to it by the FBI were national security secrets and "intelligence sources or methods" that are exempt from disclosure under FOIA; the court additionally ruled that the amount paid "reflects a confidential law enforcement technique or procedure" that also falls under a FOIA exemption.<ref name="GersteinFOIA"/>

== Inspector General Investigation ==

=== Background ===
On August 31, 2016, Amy Hess, the FBI's executive assistant director, raised concerns with the [[Office of Inspector General (United States)|Office of Inspector General]] alleging there was a disagreement between units of the Operational Technology Division (OTD) of their capability to access Farook's iPhone; namely between the Cryptographic and Electronic Analysis Unit (CEAU) and the Remote Operations Unit (ROU). She also alleged that some OTD officials were indifferent to FBI leadership (herself included)<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.fbi.gov/news/testimony/deciphering-the-debate-over-encryption|title=Statement Before the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, Subcommittee on Oversight and Investigation Washington, D.C.|last=Hess|first=Amy|date=April 19, 2016|website=fbi.gov|access-date=August 18, 2018|archive-date=February 10, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210210092059/https://www.fbi.gov/news/testimony/deciphering-the-debate-over-encryption|url-status=live}}</ref> giving possibly misleading testimony to Congress and in court orders that they had no such capability.

=== Findings ===
Ultimately, the Inspector General's March 2018 report<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://oig.justice.gov/reports/2018/o1803.pdf|title=A Special Inquiry Regarding the Accuracy of FBI Statements Concerning its Capabilities to Exploit an iPhone Seized During the San Bernardino Terror Attack Investigation|website=oig.justice.gov|publisher=Office of the Inspector General, US Department of Justice|access-date=August 18, 2018|archive-date=February 10, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210210092017/https://oig.justice.gov/reports/2018/o1803.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref> found no evidence that the OTD had withheld knowledge of the ability to unlock Farook's iPhone at the time of Director Comey's congressional testimony of February 9 and March 1, 2016. However, the report also found that poor communication and coordination between the CEAU and ROU meant that "not all relevant personnel had been engaged at the outset".

The ROU Chief (named by [[Vice Media|Vice]] to be Eric Chuang)<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.vice.com/en/article/fbi-hacking-investigations-classified-remote-operations-unit/|title=The FBI Used Classified Hacking Tools in Ordinary Criminal Investigations|last=Cox|first=Joseph|date=March 29, 2018|work=Motherboard|access-date=August 18, 2018|archive-date=February 10, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210210092238/https://www.vice.com/en/article/7xdxg9/fbi-hacking-investigations-classified-remote-operations-unit|url-status=live}}</ref> said he only became aware of the access problem after a February 11 meeting of the Digital Forensics and Analysis Section (DFAS) - of which the ROU is not a member. While the OTD directors were in frequent contact during the investigation, including discussions about Farook's iPhone, Asst. Dir. Stephen Richardson and the Chief of DFAS, John F. Bennett, believed at the time that a court order was their only alternative.

Chuang claimed the CEAU Chief didn't ask for their help due to a "line in the sand" against using classified security tools in domestic criminal cases.{{efn|Eric Chuang appears to be referring to a January 2002 memo requiring approval from the Deputy Attorney General to grant use for classified tools in criminal cases. While Chuang was aware of two previous cases where they were used, he claimed this infrequency proved that using such techniques was "difficult".}} The CEAU Chief denied such a line existed and that not using classified techniques was merely a preference. Nevertheless, the perception of this line resulted in the ROU not getting involved until after John Bennett's February 11 meeting asking "anyone" in the bureau to help.

Once Chuang "got the word out", he soon learned that a trusted vendor was "almost 90 percent of the way" to a solution after "many months" of work and asked they prioritize its completion. The unnamed vendor came forward with their solution on March 16, 2016, and successfully demonstrated it to FBI leadership on March 20. The [[United States Attorney|US Attorneys Office]] was informed the next day and they withdrew their court action against Apple on March 28.

When asked why the ROU was not involved earlier the Chief of Technical Surveillance Section (TSS), Eric Chuang's superior, initially said it was not in his "lane" and it was handled exclusively by the DFAS because "that is their mandate". He later claimed that Farook's phone was discussed from the outset but he did not instruct his unit chiefs to contact outside vendors until after February 11. In either event, neither he nor the ROU were asked to request help from their vendors until mid-February. By the time the Attorneys Office filed their February 16 court order, the ROU had only just begun contacting its vendors.

The CEAU Chief was unable to say with certainty that the ROU had been consulted beforehand and that the February 11th meeting was a final "mop-up" before a court action was filed. The CEAU's search for solutions within the FBI was undocumented and was handled informally by a senior engineer that the CEAU Chief personally trusted had checked with "everybody".

On the other hand, it's possible that Hess' asking questions is what prompted the February 11 "mop-up" meeting. During the CEAU's search Hess became concerned that she wasn't getting straight answers from the OTD and that unit chiefs didn't know the capabilities of the others. The Inspector General stated further:

{{blockquote|... the CEAU Chief may not have been interested in researching all possible solutions and instead focused only on unclassified techniques that could readily be disclosed in court that OTD and its partner agencies already had in-hand.}}

Both Hess and Chuang stated the CEAU Chief seemed not to want to use classified techniques and appeared to have an agenda in pursuing a favorable ruling against Apple. Chuang described the CEAU Chief as "definitely not happy" that they undermined his legal case against Apple and had vented his frustration with him.

Hess said the CEAU Chief wanted to use the case as a "poster child" to resolve the larger problem with encrypted devices known as the "[[Crypto Wars|Going Dark challenge]]". The challenge is defined by the FBI as "changes in technology [that] hinder law enforcement's ability to exercise investigative tools and follow critical leads".<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.fbi.gov/services/operational-technology/going-dark|title=Going Dark|website=fbi.gov|access-date=August 18, 2018|archive-date=November 1, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191101184638/https://www.fbi.gov/services/operational-technology/going-dark|url-status=live}}</ref> As The Los Angeles Times reported in March 2018, the FBI was unable to access data from 7,775 seized devices in their investigations. The unidentified method used to unlock Farook's phone - costing more than $1 million to obtain - quit working once Apple updated their operating system.<ref name="access delayed" />

=== Conclusion ===
The Inspector General's report found that statements in the FBI's testimony before Congress were accurate but relied on assumptions that the OTD units were coordinating effectively from the beginning. They also believe the miscommunication delayed finding a technical solution to accessing Farook's iPhone. The FBI disputed this since the vendor had been working on the project independently "for some time". However, according to Chuang – whom described himself as a "relationship holder" for the vendor – they were not actively working to complete the solution and that it was moved to the "front burner" on his request; to which the TSS Chief agreed.

In response to the Inspector General's report, the FBI intended to add a new OTD section to consolidate resources to address the Going Dark problem and to improve coordination between units.
